name: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
title: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
answer: Vector search stores embeddings, lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables, so retrieval can respect the same joins, filters and permissions as the rest of the data. In practice this means a product catalogue, a support ticket table and a document store can all be searched by meaning without a separate system holding a copy of the rows. The topic sits inside AI and SQL because it turns an existing database into a retrieval layer for language models and recommendation features.

sections.body: Vector search stores embeddings, lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables, so retrieval can respect the same joins, filters and permissions as the rest of the data. In practice this means a product catalogue, a support ticket table and a document store can all be searched by meaning without a separate system holding a copy of the rows. The topic sits inside AI and SQL because it turns an existing database into a retrieval layer for language models and recommendation features.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the database engine itself, most often PostgreSQL, with an extension that adds a vector column type and an index type built for nearest neighbour search. Embeddings arrive from an external model, either a hosted API or a local model, and are written into ordinary tables as arrays of floats. Because the vectors live beside the relational data, the same server, backup routine and connection pool cover both. This site is itself built from a PostgreSQL database, which is a fair illustration of how much can sit in one engine.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical build adds a vector column, backfills it by calling an embedding model over each row, and creates an approximate nearest neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat. Queries then combine a distance operator with ordinary SQL, so a filter on tenant, date or status runs in the same statement as the similarity ranking. Recall and latency are tuned through index parameters and by choosing between exact and approximate search. Teams usually evaluate retrieval quality with a held out set of queries before trusting the results in production.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Embeddings are derived from source records, so access control has to follow the vector column as closely as it follows the original table. Row level security, views and role grants in the database carry over, which is the main argument for keeping retrieval inside the engine rather than exporting a copy. Provenance matters too: teams record which model and which version produced each vector, because a model change invalidates the index and can shift results. Personal data embedded into a vector is still personal data, and deletion requests have to reach the vector row as well as the text.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is tighter coupling between retrieval and the query planner, with hybrid search that blends keyword and vector scoring in one statement. More of the surrounding work, such as chunking, embedding refresh and evaluation, is moving into database tooling rather than living in separate services. The site currently tracks 2,580 Model Context Protocol servers for SQL databases and warehouses, a sign of how many teams now expect an assistant to reach structured data directly. Expect the boundary between the database and the retrieval stack to keep thinning.
